title: Module 3 — Purpose, Vision & Direction
coreQuestion: Where am I going, why am I going there, and what must I do next?
sourceMetadata: Core Question: Where am I going, why am I going there, and what must I do next?
sourceFile: MODULE 3- PURPOSE, VISION & DIRECTION- Growth Foundation docx_034548.docx

blocks.content:
Knowing yourself is important.

Learning how to grow is important.

But a person can know themselves and continue moving without direction.

They can work hard and still work on the wrong things.

They can set goals and still pursue goals that do not matter.

They can become productive without becoming purposeful.

They can become successful according to society's definition while becoming disconnected from the life, contribution and responsibilities they actually value.

Therefore, after understanding yourself and developing a growth mindset, you must answer another important question:

Where am I going?

Purpose, vision and direction help answer that question.

Purpose helps you understand why your life, work or organization matters.

Vision helps you describe the future you want to contribute to creating.

Goals translate that vision into specific outcomes.

Objectives turn those outcomes into measurable targets.

Plans determine how you will pursue them.

Priorities determine what deserves your attention first.

Execution turns intention into reality.

A useful sequence is:

PURPOSE → VISION → GOALS → OBJECTIVES → PRIORITIES → PLAN → ACTION → MEASUREMENT → REVIEW

This module teaches you how to build that chain.

Purpose concerns the reason something exists or the contribution it is intended to make.

For an individual, purpose can be understood as the intersection of:

What matters to you;

What you are capable of developing;

The needs or problems you care about;

The people or communities you want to serve;

The contribution you want to make.

Purpose is bigger than a job title.

You may work as an engineer, teacher, entrepreneur, civil servant or consultant.

Those are roles.

Your purpose may express the broader contribution you make through those roles.

For example:

A person's job may be teaching.

Their broader contribution may be helping people develop knowledge and capability.

Another person's job may be running a business.

Their contribution may involve solving customer problems, creating employment and building useful products.

Therefore:

Role = What you do

Purpose = Why your contribution matters

lessons.title: 3.4 PURPOSE IS NOT NECESSARILY ONE JOB

blocks.content:
Consider this distinction:

PURPOSE: Why am I contributing?

VISION: What future do I want to help create?

GOAL: What important result am I pursuing?

OBJECTIVE: What measurable outcome must be achieved?

PLAN: How will I achieve it?

ACTION: What will I do now?

This distinction prevents vague ambition.

lessons.title: 3.8 YOUR VISION SHOULD BE ASPIRATIONAL AND PRACTICAL

blocks.content:
A vision should stretch you without disconnecting you completely from reality.

There is a difference between:

Aspiration

"I want to create meaningful impact."

and:

Execution

"I will develop the skills, relationships, systems and resources required to create that impact."

The vision gives direction.

The strategy gives structure.

The plan gives action.

Ask:

Is it meaningful?

Does it matter to me?

Is it understandable?

Can I explain it clearly?

Is it directional?

Does it tell me where I am going?

Is it broad enough?

Can it survive changes in job, business or circumstances?

Is it practical?

Can I identify actions that move me toward it?

Is it measurable enough?

Can I eventually determine whether I am progressing?

Do not begin by asking:

"What goals should I set?"

Begin with:

"What future am I trying to create?"

Then ask:

"What results would move me toward that future?"

This produces:

VISION → STRATEGIC GOALS

Rather than:

RANDOM DESIRES → RANDOM ACTIVITIES

This is a critical distinction.

Activity: "I will attend five business seminars."

Outcome: "I will develop and test a marketable service and acquire my first paying customers."

Activities describe what you do.

Outcomes describe what changes because of what you do.

Good planning tracks both.

Create three columns:

TABLE
Horizon | Key Question
Next 90 Days | What must I accomplish now?
Next 1–3 Years | What capability and position am I building?
Next 3–5+ Years | What larger future am I creating?

The 90-day plan should support the 1–3 year direction.

The 1–3 year direction should support the long-term vision.

Use this chain:

Vision

The future you want to create.

↓

Strategic Goal

A major result required to move toward the vision.

↓

Objective

A measurable result within a defined period.

↓

Initiative

A project or major action designed to achieve the objective.

↓

Task

A specific activity required to execute the initiative.

Example:

Vision: Become a highly capable business professional who creates value and builds sustainable enterprises.

Goal:Build strong business-development capability.

Objective: Complete a structured business-development programme and conduct 30 customer/prospect interviews within 90 days.

Initiative: Customer Discovery Project.

Tasks:

Create interview questions;

Identify prospects;

Conduct interviews;

Document findings;

Analyse patterns;

Redesign offer;

Test the revised offer.

Now the vision has become executable.

You cannot pursue everything simultaneously.

Time is limited.

Money is limited.

Energy is limited.

Attention is limited.

People are limited.

Therefore, growth requires prioritization.

Prioritization means deciding:

What matters most now?

Classify tasks into four categories:

IMPORTANT + URGENT

Do now.

IMPORTANT + NOT URGENT

Schedule deliberately.

This category often contains the activities that create long-term growth.

Examples:

Learning;

Strategic planning;

Relationship development;

Preventive maintenance;

Health;

Financial planning.

NOT IMPORTANT + URGENT

Delegate, automate or reduce where possible.

NOT IMPORTANT + NOT URGENT

Eliminate or minimize.

At the beginning of each day or week, identify:

1. The most important result

What single result would make the day/week significantly more successful?

2. The two supporting priorities

What two additional results matter most?

Then organize other activities around them.

This prevents the learner from confusing activity with progress.

Before committing time to something, ask:

Does this support my purpose?

Does this support my vision?

Does this support an important goal?

Is it urgent?

Is it important?

Can someone else do it?

Can it be automated?

What happens if I do not do it?

What happens if I do it?

Is this genuinely the best use of my current resources?

A plan is not a prison.

Circumstances change.

New information appears.

Opportunities emerge.

Markets change.

People change.

Your capabilities change.

Therefore, review your direction.

Do not abandon your purpose every time you encounter difficulty.

But do not stubbornly continue an ineffective strategy simply because you once planned it.

Use:

Purpose = relatively stable direction

Vision = desired future

Strategy = approach

Plan = current route

Actions = immediate steps

The route may change while the destination remains.

For the next 90 days, select:

1–3 major outcomes

Do not select twenty.

For each outcome define:

Outcome

What must be achieved?

Why

Why does it matter?

Measure

How will success be measured?

Deadline

When must it happen?

Capabilities

What must I learn?

Resources

What do I need?

Actions

What will I do weekly?

Evidence

What will prove progress?

Risks

What could stop me?

Response

What will I do if that happens?

Every week ask:

RESULTS

What did I accomplish?

PROGRESS

What moved forward?

FAILURES

What did not work?

LEARNING

What did I learn?

PRIORITIES

What matters most next week?

CAPABILITY

What skill do I need to develop?

ADJUSTMENT

What should I stop, start or continue?

This creates a continuous planning cycle.

lessons.title: 3.29 PURPOSE, VISION AND DIRECTION FOR DIFFERENT PEOPLE

blocks.content:
The framework applies broadly.

FOR AN INDIVIDUAL

Purpose → personal vision → development goals → career/life plan.

FOR A PROFESSIONAL

Purpose → professional vision → capability goals → career strategy.

FOR AN ENTREPRENEUR

Purpose → business vision → strategic objectives → execution plan.

FOR A BUSINESS

Purpose → organizational vision → strategic goals → departmental objectives → KPIs.

FOR AN NGO

Purpose → impact vision → programme objectives → implementation plan → impact measures.

FOR GOVERNMENT

Public purpose → desired societal outcome → policy objectives → programmes → implementation → public-value measurement.

The underlying logic remains the same.

Mistake 1 — Copying someone else's vision

Your vision must be appropriate to your own responsibility and context.

Mistake 2 — Confusing possessions with purpose

Money and assets can be legitimate goals, but they do not answer every question about contribution.

Mistake 3 — Creating too many goals

Too many priorities often produce weak execution.

Mistake 4 — Setting goals without capabilities

Ask what you must learn to achieve the goal.

Mistake 5 — Planning without execution

A plan is not progress until action begins.

Mistake 6 — Refusing to adapt

Changing the strategy is not necessarily abandoning the vision.

Mistake 7 — Measuring activity instead of outcomes

Being busy is not the same as making progress.

Mistake 8 — Setting goals only because they sound impressive

A goal should matter, not merely look impressive.

lessons.title: 3.31 PRACTICAL TOOL — THE PURPOSE DISCOVERY WORKSHEET

blocks.content:
Complete the following.

WHAT MATTERS TO ME?

The issues I care deeply about:

WHAT AM I GOOD AT?

My strongest capabilities:

WHAT CAN I DEVELOP?

Capabilities I could become excellent at:

WHAT PROBLEMS INTEREST ME?

Problems I would like to help solve:

WHO DO I WANT TO SERVE?

People/groups/markets/institutions I want to contribute to:

WHAT CONTRIBUTION DO I WANT TO MAKE?

I want to help:

by:

so that:

Using the information above, draft:

My purpose is to __________________________________________ so that __________________________________________.

Then ask:

Is this authentic?

Is it meaningful?

Does it reflect contribution?

Can I live it through different roles?

Does it help me make better decisions?

Revise it until it is clear.

Imagine your life several years from now.

Describe:

CHARACTER

Who have I become?

KNOWLEDGE

What do I understand?

SKILLS

What can I do exceptionally well?

CAREER

What kind of work am I doing?

BUSINESS

What have I built, if applicable?

FINANCES

What level of financial capability and stability have I developed?

RELATIONSHIPS

What relationships have I built and maintained?

HEALTH

How do I take care of myself?

SERVICE

Who benefits from my work?

IMPACT

What is better because of my contribution?

LEGACY

What am I building that can continue beyond me?

Complete:

"I envision becoming ________________________________. I will use my capabilities to ________________________________. I will build/contribute to ________________________________. The people/institutions I serve will ________________________________. I want my work and life to contribute to ________________________________."

Now convert the vision into goals.

TABLE
Vision Area | 3–5 Year Direction | 1-Year Goal | 90-Day Objective
Personal |  |  | 
Career |  |  | 
Business |  |  | 
Financial |  |  | 
Skills |  |  | 
Relationships |  |  | 
Health |  |  | 
Contribution |  |  | 

Do not force every category if it is irrelevant.

The purpose is to create balanced direction, not artificial goals.

The final submission should contain:

1. Personal Context

2. Purpose Discovery Analysis

3. Purpose Statement

4. Personal Vision

5. 3–5 Year Direction

6. One-Year Goals

7. 90-Day Objectives

8. Personal Development Plan

9. Priority System

10. Personal Scorecard

11. Weekly Accountability System

12. Personal Commitment

Recommended final format:

Personal Purpose, Vision & Direction Blueprint

Total: 100 Marks

TABLE
Assessment Area | Marks
Self-reflection and context | 10
Purpose discovery | 15
Purpose statement | 10
Vision development | 15
Long-term direction | 10
Goal quality | 10
90-day objectives | 10
Personal development plan | 10
Prioritization and measurement | 5
Practicality and coherence | 5
TOTAL | 100

For seven consecutive days, spend 20–30 minutes working on your direction.

DAY 1

Write what matters most to you.

DAY 2

Identify your strengths and capabilities.

DAY 3

Identify the problems you want to help solve.

DAY 4

Draft your purpose statement.

DAY 5

Draft your vision.

DAY 6

Convert the vision into goals.

DAY 7

Create your first 90-day action plan.

At the end of seven days, you should have a first version of your Personal Growth Blueprint.

It does not need to be perfect.

It needs to be usable.

Your direction should be reviewed regularly.

DAILY

What matters most today?

WEEKLY

Am I progressing?

MONTHLY

What results have I produced?

QUARTERLY

Am I still pursuing the right priorities?

ANNUALLY

Has my direction changed because I have learned more?

This creates a living development system rather than a document that is written once and forgotten.

Before making a major decision, ask:

PURPOSE

Does this align with why I want to contribute?

VISION

Does it move me toward the future I want?

GOALS

Does it support an important objective?

CAPABILITY

Will it help me develop something valuable?

RESOURCES

Can I afford the required time, money and attention?

RISK

What could go wrong?

OPPORTUNITY

What could become possible?

PRIORITY

Is this more important than what I would have to postpone?

RESULT

What measurable value could this create?

If the answer is consistently "no," reconsider the decision.

lessons.title: 3.45 THE SCHOOL OF GROWTH GLOBAL DIRECTION MODEL

blocks.content:
Remember:

PURPOSE

Why do I exist/contribute?

↓

VISION

What future do I want to help create?

↓

GOALS

What important results will move me there?

↓

OBJECTIVES

What measurable results must I achieve now?

↓

PRIORITIES

What deserves my limited resources first?

↓

PLAN

How will I achieve it?

↓

ACTION

What will I do today?

↓

MEASUREMENT

What evidence shows progress?

↓

REVIEW

What should I continue, improve, stop or start?

This is how an idea becomes a direction.

You do not need to have your entire life figured out today.

You need enough clarity to know what matters, what direction you are moving in and what responsible action comes next.

Your vision may become clearer as you learn.

Your strategy may change.

Your career may change.

Your business may change.

Your environment may change.

But intentional living requires that you periodically stop and ask:

Where am I going?

Why does it matter?

What must I become?

What must I build?

What must I learn?

What should I prioritize?

What must I do now?

Purpose gives meaning.

Vision gives direction.

Goals create focus.

Objectives create measurement.

Priorities protect attention.

Plans organize action.

Execution produces evidence.

Review creates learning.

That is how intention becomes progress.

Do not merely dream about your future.

Design a direction.

Develop the capacity required for that direction.

Take action.

Measure what happens.

Learn.

Adapt.

Continue.

MODULE 3 COMPLETION STANDARD

You have completed this module when you can clearly articulate:

WHY you want to contribute.

WHAT future you want to create.

WHAT results matter most.

WHAT capabilities you must develop.

WHAT you must prioritize.

WHAT you will do during the next 90 days.

How you will measure your progress.

The objective is not to predict your entire future.

The objective is to become capable of intentionally designing and continuously improving your direction.

SCHOOL OF GROWTH GLOBAL

Leadership. Strategy. Transformation.

Growth Foundation
